awd_titl_txt: Conference: How SynBio can realistically impact crop improvement and agriculture
awd_abstract_narration:
Synthetic biology has significant potential in plant agriculture, for example, by providing new trait genes to breeding programs, engineering plant-microbe interactions, and developing new crops and products. This Workshop brings together a number of different communities such as established, public- and private-sector plant breeders and metabolic engineers as well as early-career plant synthetic biology researchers such as faculty, postdoctoral researchers, and PhD student trainees to catalyze interactions that will help the field reach its potential positive impact on science and society. The workshop forum provides an opportunity for the participants from these different communities, to learn from and network with each other, and to leave with fresh, down-to-earth, actionable perspectives and contacts. The format of the workshop would include keynote talks, short talks, idea pitches and posters, as well as panel and breakout discussion sessions. After the workshop, a report will be prepared and circulated within the plant synthetic biology community.

This Workshop brings together early-career synthetic biology researchers, agricultural synthetic biology and agribusiness professionals as well as postdoctoral researchers and graduate students. The format is a lively mix of talks highlighting realistic opportunities and challenges and showcasing real-world applications. Also included are idea-pitches from early career researchers and live feedback from professionals, posters and breakout sessions. The end point will be a crafting of a report to project the Workshop’s message to the plant synthetic biology community. The aim above all is to give participants from different communities opportunities to learn from and network with each other, and to leave with fresh, down-to-earth, actionable perspectives and contacts.

This award is co-funded by the Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences, the Systems and Synthetic Biology Program, the Cellular and Biochemical Engineering Program and the Plant Genome Research Program.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This conference examined how synthetic biology (SynBio) can realistically contribute to crop improvement and agriculture. While SynBio has generated tremendous excitement for its potential to transform plant science, this project focused on separating near‑term, achievable impacts from longer‑term aspirations and  on identifying what is required for successful translation of research into agricultural practice.

Held in early 2025, the NSF‑supported conference brought together approximately 40 early‑career researchers (from graduate students to new faculty members) alongside experienced scientists from industry, universities, and the public sector. A central goal was to address a long‑standing disconnect between SynBio researchers, who often have an engineering background, and agricultural scientists. As summarized in an editorial in Plant Physiology, a leading journal for plant sciences, the two groups often work with different organisms, timelines, incentives, and technical languages. By placing these communities in direct conversation, the conference created a rare opportunity to align expectations, priorities, and definitions of success.

A key intellectual outcome was a shared understanding that effective crop engineering requires deeper integration of SynBio with foundational plant and agricultural science. Discussions highlighted that many promising tools—such as genome editing, synthetic gene circuits, and metabolic engineering—cannot reliably deliver agricultural benefits without accounting for plant development, environmental variability, breeding constraints, and field‑level performance. Participants emphasized the importance of building biological methods that are robust, scalable, and economically viable in real agricultural settings.

The discussions also clarified the importance of clearly defined value propositions for agricultural innovation. Unlike laboratory research, agriculture operates at large scales, under variable environmental conditions, and with narrow margins for risk. Speakers and breakout groups discussed how synthetic biology solutions must be evaluated against existing breeding and management approaches, using measurable outcomes rather than optimistic claims. This emphasis on realism helped participants identify research directions where SynBio is most likely to add unique value, as well as areas where alternative solutions may be more effective.

Broader impacts were a core strength of the project. Early‑career researchers played central roles throughout the conference, gaining exposure to agricultural challenges, industry perspectives, and translational pathways that are often missing from academic training. The meeting fostered professional development by encouraging participants to think across disciplines and career sectors, and by modeling constructive, evidence‑based communication about the limits as well as the promise of new technologies. A small group of early career researchers had the chance to pitch their best plant biotechnology ideas to a panel of industry experts and receive live feedback, in a Shark Tank-style competition.

Overall, this award supported a timely and impactful assessment of how synthetic biology can contribute to sustainable agriculture. By bringing together diverse stakeholders, centering early‑career researchers, and focusing on realistic outcomes, the conference advanced both scientific understanding and responsible innovation. The discussions and new interdisciplinary connections formed during this project are expected to inform future research, training, and collaboration aimed at delivering tangible benefits for agriculture and society. In particular, the participants identified the need for more scientific resources, including more “collision spaces” where researchers, breeders, growers, and industry scientists can regularly interact. Such interactions were identified as essential for guiding research toward problems that maximize societal benefits as the field matures.
